lede: Numb, tingling fingers that wake you at night? Our certified hand therapist helps take pressure off the median nerve so you can sleep and use your hands with less trouble.
what_it_is: The carpal tunnel is a narrow passageway in the wrist, about an inch wide according to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS). Small wrist bones form its floor and sides, and a stiff band called the transverse carpal ligament forms the roof. The median nerve shares this tight space with the tendons that bend your fingers. When pressure inside the tunnel rises, the nerve gets squeezed. That squeeze is carpal tunnel syndrome.

It is a common problem. Cleveland Clinic estimates that about 3 out of every 1,000 people in the U.S. develop it each year. Women and older adults are more likely to have it, and so are people with diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, or thyroid conditions. Pregnancy can bring it on through swelling, and long hours of repetitive hand motion or vibrating tools add to the load on the nerve.
symptoms: Numbness or tingling in the thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers
Symptoms that wake you up at night
Brief shock-like sensations that shoot into the fingers
Burning or aching in the hand or wrist
Weak pinch or grip, or dropping things
Clumsiness with small tasks such as buttons
A little finger that usually feels normal
causes: A carpal tunnel that is naturally smaller (it can run in families)
Repeating the same hand and wrist motions for long periods
Holding the wrist bent far up or down
Diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, or thyroid imbalance
A previous wrist fracture or swelling from an injury

how_therapy_helps.intro: Therapy for carpal tunnel aims to lower pressure on the median nerve, especially during the hours it is most irritated. The physical therapy clinical practice guideline published in the Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy (JOSPT) recommends a wrist orthosis that holds the wrist in a neutral position at night for short-term symptom relief and better function. The American Society of Hand Therapists (ASHT) adds activity changes, education, and specific exercises. If your evaluation suggests more severe nerve involvement, we share that with your physician.
methods: Laura Drumm, CHT, fabricates a splint in the clinic that keeps your wrist straight while you sleep, the neutral position the JOSPT guideline recommends.
If night wear alone does not control symptoms, the guideline supports adding wear during the daytime tasks that provoke them in mild to moderate cases.
Gentle sequences of arm, wrist, and finger positions help the median nerve slide through the tunnel. The AAOS lists them among nonsurgical treatments.
We look at how you grip, type, and use tools, then work on a lighter grip, a neutral wrist at the keyboard, and regular breaks.
You learn which positions and habits load the nerve, so you can head off flare-ups on your own between visits.
If you have surgery, we follow your surgeon's protocol to restore motion, grip, and pinch, and we keep the surgeon updated.

first_visit: Your first visit takes about an hour, with evaluation and treatment the same day. Laura maps where the numbness and tingling occur, tests light-touch sensation in your fingertips, and measures grip and pinch strength. Provocative tests such as the Phalen test and Tinel sign show how irritable the nerve is. She also checks your neck and arm so other nerve problems are not missed, then fits your splint and starts your home program.
recovery: How quickly symptoms ease depends on how long they have been present and how much pressure the nerve is under. The JOSPT guideline describes night splinting as a short-term relief strategy, so it works best paired with changes in how you use your hands. If you need surgery, the AAOS reports that grip and pinch strength usually return in about 2 to 3 months, or 6 to 12 months when the nerve was severely compressed. Numbness can take several months to improve, and complete recovery can take up to a year.
self_care: Keep your wrist straight while you sleep instead of curled under your pillow or chin.
Use a relaxed grip and take short breaks to gently stretch your hands during repetitive tasks.
Set up your keyboard so your wrists are not bent sharply up or down.
Notice which tasks bring on tingling and space them out or change how you do them.
see_a_doctor: Numbness that no longer comes and goes, since the AAOS warns that untreated compression can lead to permanent loss of sensation
Weakness or frequent dropping of objects that is getting worse
Symptoms that interfere with your sleep or usual activities (Mayo Clinic)
Numbness or tingling that begins after a wrist injury or fracture

faqs.q: Can carpal tunnel go away on its own?
faqs.a: Sometimes, when the cause is temporary. Swelling during pregnancy is a common example, and the JOSPT physical therapy guideline recommends a wrist splint during pregnancy with a follow-up check after delivery. When pressure on the median nerve continues, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons warns that untreated carpal tunnel syndrome can cause permanent numbness and weakness, so symptoms that persist deserve an evaluation.

faqs.q: Does wearing a wrist brace at night help carpal tunnel?
faqs.a: Night bracing is one of the best-supported first steps. The physical therapy clinical practice guideline in JOSPT recommends a wrist orthosis that holds the wrist in a neutral, straight position at night for short-term relief and better hand function. Position matters, because the AAOS lists bending the wrist far up or down as a risk factor. A hand therapist can check the fit or make a custom splint.

faqs.q: What exercises help carpal tunnel syndrome?
faqs.a: Nerve gliding exercises are a common choice, and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons lists them among nonsurgical treatments. The JOSPT physical therapy guideline rates the research on nerve mobilization as mixed, and it supports combining a splint with a stretching program in mild to moderate cases. Gliding exercises should feel gentle. If one increases tingling, it needs to be scaled back.

faqs.a: First Rehabilitation of North Palm Beach accepts Medicare and most major insurance plans for hand therapy. Coverage details such as copays and visit limits vary by plan, so our front desk verifies your benefits before you start. Call 561-624-4263 with your insurance information, and we will let you know what your plan covers for carpal tunnel care.

faqs.q: What does a certified hand therapist do for carpal tunnel?
faqs.a: A certified hand therapist (CHT) is an occupational or physical therapist with advanced training in the hand and upper limb. According to the American Society of Hand Therapists, care for carpal tunnel includes a full evaluation to find the root cause, night bracing to keep the wrist in a safe position, splinting during aggravating activities, education on activity changes, and specific exercises for recovery and prevention.

faqs.q: How do I know if hand numbness is carpal tunnel or something else?
faqs.a: Carpal tunnel numbness usually involves the thumb, index, middle, and part of the ring finger, and Mayo Clinic notes the little finger is typically spared. Numbness in the little finger, or symptoms that start in the neck, can point to a different nerve. Only a physician can diagnose the cause. A hand therapy evaluation documents your symptom pattern and shares the findings with your doctor.

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 G56.0 verified on icd10data.com; it is a category header. Billable codes are G56.00 (unspecified), G56.01 (right), G56.02 (left), G56.03 (bilateral).

The JOSPT CTS guideline cited is the 2019 version (Erickson et al). A 2026 revision (doi 10.2519/jospt.2026.0301) appears to exist; I could not review its full text. Please confirm the night neutral orthosis recommendation still stands as worded.
The guideline section on nerve and tendon gliding could not be read in full; nerve gliding is attributed to AAOS OrthoInfo only. Clinician should confirm comfort with presenting it as a core method.
Prevalence figure (about 3 per 1,000 per year) comes from Cleveland Clinic. NINDS page returned a server error and was not used.
First visit mentions Phalen and Tinel tests and a neck and arm screen; adjust to Laura's actual exam routine.

Fact-check: the 2019 JOSPT CPG rates evidence on neurodynamic (nerve gliding) mobilization as conflicting (grade D); the exercises FAQ now says so. Confirm you are comfortable keeping nerve gliding as a listed method.
